title: Your Spouse Should Not Have to Compete With a Screen for Your Eyes, Your Laughter, and Your Attention
paragraphs: Your Spouse Should Not Have to Compete With a Screen for Your Eyes, Your Laughter, and Your Attention

Some marriages do not begin breaking with an affair, a screaming match, or divorce papers. Sometimes the distance begins with two people sitting inches apart… while one of them keeps giving the best of their attention to something glowing in their hand.
Your spouse says something.
“Hmm?”
They repeat it.
You answer without looking up.
A few seconds later, you laugh.
But not because of anything they said.
Something on the screen made you laugh.
And across the room—or perhaps only twelve inches away—the person you once could not stop looking at quietly feels something they may not even know how to explain.
I miss you.
Except you are right there.
That may be one of the strangest forms of loneliness in modern marriage.
To be beside someone who is somewhere else.
To sleep next to someone whose final attention before closing their eyes belongs to a screen.
To wake beside someone whose first reach of the morning is not toward you, not toward prayer, not toward the Word of God…
but toward a phone.
No affair.
No secret hotel room.
No dramatic betrayal.
Nothing that looks scandalous enough to make people gasp.
Just five minutes here.
Ten minutes there.
One more video.
One more notification.
One more comment.
One more scroll.
One more “hold on.”
One more “I’m listening” while your eyes say you are not.
And that is precisely why this can become dangerous.
Because some forms of marital neglect do not arrive like an explosion.
They accumulate like dust.
Almost invisible.
Until one day somebody realizes they have been emotionally starving in a house full of food.
Scripture spoke to the heart of this problem long before smartphones existed.
Paul wrote in Philippians 2:4:
“μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστοι σκοποῦντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων ἕκαστοι.”
A faithful sense of the Greek is:
Do not each look only to your own things, but also to the things of others.
That word translated “looking,” σκοποῦντες — skopountes, comes from skopeō: to look at, pay attention to, take notice of, or carefully regard.
And notice the context.

Paul is not giving married couples a command specifically about phones. He is teaching the church the Christ-shaped posture of humility. In the surrounding verses, believers are called away from selfish ambition and empty glory, toward considering others and their concerns. Then Paul brings everything to its breathtaking center:
Jesus Christ.
“τοῦτο φρονεῖτε ἐν ὑμῖν ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ…”
Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.
Then Paul points us toward the humility of the Son of God—the One who took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient even to death on a cross.
So Philippians 2:4 is bigger than digital etiquette.
This is not merely…
Put your phone down because phones are bad.
Phones are tools.
Social media is a tool.
Technology is a tool.
The deeper question is:
What receives your attention so consistently that the person God entrusted to your covenant begins receiving what is left over?
That question hurts.
Because perhaps you would never cheat on your spouse.
But would you repeatedly ignore them?
Perhaps you would never abandon your marriage.
But have you gradually stopped being present inside it?
Perhaps you would never flirt with somebody else across a dinner table.
But do you spend dinner staring into a device while the person you promised your life to eats across from you?
You can be faithful with your body and still become careless with your presence.
You can provide financially and still leave someone emotionally hungry.
You can say “I love you” every morning and slowly train your spouse to believe that everything on your screen is more interesting than whatever is happening inside their heart.
And sometimes the neglected spouse stops complaining.
That is not always good news.
Sometimes people stop complaining because something improved.
Sometimes they stop because they became tired of asking.
There is a difference.
There is a kind of silence that is peace.
And there is another kind of silence that is resignation.
Maybe your husband used to tell you about his day in detail.
Now he says, “It was fine.”
Maybe your wife used to crawl close to you on the couch.
Now she sits at the other end with her own phone.
Maybe you think, See? She does it too.
Maybe you think, He is just as bad.
Perhaps.
But Philippians 2 does not invite us to wait until somebody else becomes humble first.
Jesus did not love us because we had finally become lovable enough.
The Gospel confronts the exhausting mathematics of marriage:
I will give when you give.
I will listen when you listen.
I will apologize when you apologize.
I will change when you change.
Christ interrupts that cycle.
The cross says grace moves first.
And perhaps tonight repentance looks surprisingly ordinary.
Maybe there are no tears at an altar.
No dramatic music.
No public confession.
Maybe repentance sounds like a phone being placed facedown on a table.
And then a sentence:
“Talk to me. I want to hear you.”
Maybe it looks like noticing the expression on your spouse's face instead of the notification at the top of your screen.
Maybe it sounds like:
“I think I have been here physically without really being here. I’m sorry.”
Do not underestimate those words.
Because one of the most healing experiences in a marriage is not having a perfect spouse.
It is having a spouse who can still be convicted.
A spouse who can recognize hurt without immediately defending themselves.
A spouse who can say:
“I see what I have been doing.”
“I understand why that hurt.”
“I don't want you begging for my attention anymore.”
“Please forgive me.”
There is something deeply Christlike about turning toward someone.
Jesus repeatedly noticed people others overlooked.
The desperate.
The grieving.
The ashamed.
The socially inconvenient.
The people everyone else had learned to walk past.
He saw them.
And although marriage is not the direct subject of every Gospel scene where Jesus notices someone, His character exposes something in us:
Love pays attention.
Love notices.
Love is not merely an emotion hidden somewhere inside your chest.
Biblical love moves outward.
It serves.
It listens.
It considers.
It gives.
And yes, sometimes love says:
“This can wait.”
That email can wait.
That reel can wait.
That argument in the comment section can wait.
That video can wait.
That notification can wait.
The person sitting in front of you will not always be sitting there.
Read that again.
Not because tragedy is guaranteed tomorrow.
But because marriage is mortal.
Life moves.
Bodies age.
Children grow.
Seasons disappear.
The ordinary Tuesday nights you barely notice today may become memories you would someday give almost anything to revisit.
One day you may miss the voice interrupting your scrolling.
You may miss the question you once found inconvenient.
You may miss hearing your name called from another room.
You may miss those feet on your side of the bed.
You may even miss the stories you thought you had heard a thousand times.
So why wait until absence teaches you the value of presence?
Your spouse should not have to become more entertaining than the internet to deserve your eyes.
They should not have to compete with an algorithm engineered to keep offering you something new.
They should not need perfect hair, perfect conversation, perfect humor, perfect energy, or perfect sexuality to hold the attention of the person who made a covenant with them.
Marriage is not an endless audition.
Your husband should not have to perform for your attention.
Your wife should not have to become content.
And perhaps this article is making you uncomfortable because you know exactly which side of this conversation you are on.
Maybe you are the one holding the phone.
If so, conviction is not condemnation.
In Christ, exposure can become the doorway to repentance.
Do something with what God is showing you.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
Put it down.
Look at them.
Ask a real question.
Then listen long enough for the first answer to become the second answer.
Because “How are you?” often gets “fine.”
But presence sometimes eventually gets the truth.
Or maybe you are the spouse who has been staring at the side of somebody's face for months.
You have tried joking about it.
You have tried competing with it.
You have tried becoming quiet.
You have wondered whether you are boring.
Unattractive.
Too needy.
Too emotional.
Too much.
Please hear this carefully: this article is not permission to weaponize Scripture against your spouse.
Do not shove Philippians 2:4 across the table like ammunition.
The Word of God is not a club for winning marital arguments.
It is first a mirror.
Before saying, “This verse describes you,” ask:
“Lord, where does this verse expose me?”
Maybe your distraction is not a phone.
Maybe it is work.
Gaming.
Television.
Sports.
Ministry.
Friends.
Hobbies.
Even something good can become disordered when it continually receives the attention that love requires us to steward elsewhere.
And yes…
even ministry.
You can speak about Jesus publicly while neglecting the person you vowed to love privately.
You can answer strangers in a comment section while refusing to answer the ache sitting beside you.
You can encourage thousands and ignore one.
That should sober every Christian with a platform—including us.
Because the Gospel does not merely transform what we post.
The Gospel must transform how we live when nobody is watching.
Jesus did not die merely to improve our online behavior.
He died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He calls us to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He reconciles us to God.
And the grace that saves us begins reshaping the ordinary corners of our lives—including the way we speak, listen, forgive, serve, repent, and love inside marriage.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Sometimes the scandal is obvious.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Deception.
Abandonment.
Betrayal.
Sometimes it is quieter.
A thousand tiny moments of indifference.
A marriage slowly disappearing behind two illuminated screens.
But grace can enter there too.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin did not happen.
Not by calling neglect harmless.
Not by demanding that wounded people fake healing.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace repents.
Grace forgives.
Grace rebuilds.
Grace teaches us to love differently.
Maybe your marriage does not need another expensive vacation as desperately as it needs twenty uninterrupted minutes tonight.
Maybe you do not need a new spouse.
Maybe you need new habits.
Maybe the first battlefield is not the bedroom.
Maybe it is the dinner table.
Maybe restoration begins with two phones placed somewhere neither person can reach without standing up.
And maybe the first conversation is awkward.
Have it anyway.
“Have I made you feel like my phone matters more than you?”
Then do something terrifying.
Do not defend yourself.
Listen.
If the answer hurts, listen.
If your spouse cries, listen.
If they say, “I stopped telling you things because you never seemed interested,” listen.
If they say, “I feel alone even when you're here,” do not immediately explain your intentions.
Intentions matter.
But so does impact.
Then ask:
“What would being more present look like to you?”
That is not weakness.
That is love learning how to pay attention again.
And if both of you have failed?
Welcome to marriage between two sinners who need Jesus.
There is grace for that.
The Christian marriage was never supposed to be the story of two flawless human beings.
It is two people continually discovering how desperately they need the mercy of Christ.
Confessing.
Forgiving.
Learning.
Failing.
Getting back up.
Returning to Jesus.
Returning to each other.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Perhaps you need to send this article to your spouse.
But before you do, ask yourself whether you are sending it as an accusation…
or an invitation.
There is a difference between:
“READ THIS. THIS IS YOU.”
and:
“I read this and realized there are things I need to change too. Can we talk tonight?”
One starts a trial.
The other may start healing.
And perhaps you know another couple living this without having words for it.
Not to shame anyone.
Send it privately to a couple you love.
Save it before the feed carries it away, because conviction is easy to feel for three minutes and easier to forget by morning.
Maybe your marriage has survived this.
Maybe you are fighting through it now.
Maybe you have been the distracted spouse.
Maybe you have been the lonely one.
Maybe both are true.
You do not have to tell strangers every private detail.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment pretending finally loses its grip.
And if you know Christ has already begun restoring something you thought was dying, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another couple's reason not to give up.
It does not.
It does not.
Christian giving must not be manipulated. Scripture says giving is to come from what a person has determined in the heart, not from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But voluntary support can still become a meaningful offering toward Gospel work.
It helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building.
Keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.

And sometimes glorifying God with what He has entrusted to us includes freely supporting Gospel work we believe is bearing good fruit—not under pressure, not to purchase blessing, but from gratitude and willing generosity.
One share can enter a home we have never seen.
One tag can reach a husband who has stopped noticing the distance.
One private message can reach a wife who thought nobody understood.
One comment can make another believer brave enough to admit, “Us too.”
One saved article can be reopened on the night somebody finally decides to put the phone down and have the conversation.
Put the screen down long enough to see the soul beside you.
Look into the eyes you once searched across crowded rooms.
Listen to the voice you once stayed awake late just to hear.
Ask what has been hurting.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive what can be forgiven.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help when wounds run deeper than a conversation can repair.
And bring the marriage back beneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not merely less screen time.
The goal is more Christlike love.
Not merely fewer notifications.
More attention.
Not merely digital boundaries.
A heart being transformed.
Not merely saving a marriage's appearance.
Learning again to see the person inside it.
Your phone will eventually become obsolete.
The posts will disappear down the feed.
The videos will be forgotten.
Today's urgent notification will become tomorrow's digital dust.
But the person sitting beside you is carrying a soul.
A story.
Fears they may not have told you.
Prayers you may not know they pray.
Wounds you may not realize you caused.
Love they may still be desperately trying to give you.
So tonight, when the screen lights up…
perhaps let it wait.
Turn toward them.
Look.
Listen.
Stay.
And remember this:
Do not wait until an empty chair teaches you how precious the person sitting in it was.
